justification_quote: Sec. 1 (p.1): 'in biological brains long-term learning is thought to occur (Martin et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2012) primarily through synaptic plasticity' - the biology is citation-only; the paper runs no biological evidence of its own.
note: External E3: Martin/Grimwood/Morris 2000 evaluates the synaptic-plasticity-and-memory hypothesis and finds a wealth of data supporting necessity (sufficiency less supported) - independent literature evidence exists for the T1 claim; cited in-paper as well.

justification_quote: Sec. 2 states the mapping (Eqs. 1-2: 'the Hebbian trace is simply a running average of the product of pre- and post-synaptic activity'); Sec. 4.2 (Fig. 3) runs a matched comparison - 'performance on the exact same problem, architecture, and parameters, but restoring plastic connections'; Sec. 4.5 (Fig. 6) runs 'full differentiable plasticity, no plasticity at all, and homogenous plasticity... Everything else is identical between all three conditions'.
note: The manipulated variable in Secs. 4.2/4.3/4.5 is the bio-inspired plasticity component itself (removed, homogenized, or restored at matched parameters), showing the component carries the mapped Hebbian computation's function rather than the name being decorative.

justification_quote: Sec. 4.2 (Fig. 3): non-plastic RNN 'error essentially flatlines at a high level', LSTM solves in ~500k episodes vs plastic net below .01 error within 2,000 episodes with 51 vs 2,050 neurons; Sec. 4.5 (Fig. 6): three conditions identical except plasticity, 'For each condition, we perform 15 runs with different random seeds'.
note: Capacity confound controlled against the mechanism: the plastic network wins with far fewer neurons (51 vs 2,050), and the no-plasticity condition is matched in all else.

justification_quote: Gain is tested across task families with the paper's own controls: binary pattern memorization (Sec. 4.2), natural-image memorization with independent-vs-shared-alpha ablation (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 5), maze RL with the three-condition ablation (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 6); Omniglot (Table 1) is a baseline comparison only, with no plasticity-removed control in that family.
note: Multi-family evidence with own ablations; no scale variation beyond 1,000-bit/1,024-pixel patterns; Omniglot shows 'competitive' rather than superior results (98.3% vs MAML 98.7%), recorded as a limit of the generality evidence.

justification_quote: Abstract claims map one-to-one onto controlled experiments: 'traditional non-plastic recurrent networks fail to solve this task' (Sec. 4.2, Fig. 3), 'plastic networks outperform a non-plastic equivalent in a maze exploration task' (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 6); claims are explicitly scoped ('in a maze exploration task', 'such as the Omniglot task') and the conclusion says 'may provide'.

justification_quote: Abstract's improvement claim ('plastic networks outperform a non-plastic equivalent in a maze exploration task'; 'traditional non-plastic recurrent networks fail to solve this task') most rests on attributing the gain to synaptic plasticity rather than to capacity or architecture - the T3 attribution.

justification_quote: Sec. 1 (p.1): 'Neurobiological research underscores the critical role of dendrites in integrating synaptic inputs, thereby significantly enhancing the information processing capabilities of neurons (Kampa and Stuart, 2006; Smith, Smith, Branco and Häusser, 2013; Gidon... 2020)' and 'the computing function of the individual pyramidal neuron can be mapped to an abstracted two-layer neural network (Poirazi, Brannon and Mel, 2003)' - biology is citation-only.
note: External E3: London and Häusser 2005 is the canonical independent review establishing that dendrites perform active computation; the cited paper itself presents no biological measurements.

justification_quote: Sec. 3.1 states the mapping (Eqs. 2-4: apical and basal dendritic potentials conducted to soma, 'the MCN model integrates this information to the somatic potential'); Sec. 4.3 (Fig. 10-11, Table 4) replaces the MCN with parameter-matched point neurons - 'In order to maintain consistency with the parameter count of the MCN model, each group consisted of 512 LI neurons' - and swaps population encoding for cosine embedding; both manipulations degrade performance.
note: The manipulated variables are the two bio-inspired components themselves (dendritic compartment structure; population encoding), each replaced by a matched non-compartmental / non-population alternative at equal parameters; the compartmental mechanism carries the mapped integration function.

justification_quote: Sec. 4.1: 'All models were trained under the same experimental conditions, detailed in Table 1... Each model was tested in ten independent runs' (Table 2, 19 Atari games); Sec. 4.3: 'We train all three models with the same parameter settings and run ten rounds of testing experiments for each model' (Table 4) - the gain is isolated to the MCN and population-encoding components with parameter-matched controls.
note: Capacity confound explicitly controlled (LI neuron groups matched to MCN parameter count); Table 7 additionally shows hyperparameter sensitivity is limited, so the gain is not a tuning artifact.

justification_quote: Beyond the Atari RL setting, Sec. 5.2 (Table 6) shows MCN beats parameter-matched LIF and LI models on MNIST (97.32 vs 96.80/93.81), sequential MNIST (94.61 vs 90.07/84.36) and Spiking Heidelberg Digits (89.39 vs 63.11/48.80) - the mechanism's gain is replicated across RL and two classification task families with matched controls.
note: Generality evidence spans 19 Atari games plus 3 classification datasets; the SHD temporal task shows the largest gap; no scale-up beyond these benchmarks is tested.

justification_quote: Abstract's ablation sentence matches Table 4 directly ('the proposed multi-compartment neuron model and the quantile fraction implicit population spike representation significantly enhance the performance'); 'surpasses the vanilla FQF model' holds in aggregate over the 19-game evaluation, and the paper itself reports 'our model's scores are slightly lower than those of the FQF model in five tasks' (Sec. 4.1).
note: scope_match = match, with a recorded caveat: the 'surpasses' claim is aggregate across the suite (FQF wins 5 of 19 games, e.g. Asteroids, BeamRider, Breakout, KungFuMaster), not uniform per-game superiority; the abstract does not claim per-game wins.

justification_quote: Abstract's improvement claim ('surpasses the vanilla FQF model... as well as the Spiking-FQF models') and its ablation sentence both attribute the gain to the MCN model and population spike representation - the attribution of performance to the bio-inspired correspondence is the load-bearing transition.

justification_quote: Sec. 1: 'A popular theory in cognitive science about how the brain handles multimodal information is the Global Workspace Theory (Baars, 1988; Dehaene et al., 1998)' - the brain/cognition side is citation-only; no biological or cognitive experiment is run in this paper.
note: External E3: Dehaene and Changeux 2011 (Neuron) reviews converging neuroimaging and neurophysiological evidence for a global neuronal workspace - independent literature evidence for the T1 claim.

justification_quote: Sec. 3.1 states the mapping (encoders/decoders implement alignment and broadcast: 'the GW model optimizes the desired criteria of multimodal representation alignment and broadcast'); Sec. 2 ablates the GW-specific computation: 'we also remove the broadcast property (the ability to project global-workspace information back to each specialized module), leading to a contrastive-alignment version of our model similar to CLIP... both manipulations severely impair our model's ability to transfer policies between modalities' (Fig. 3: CLIP-like and GW w/o cycles fail transfer in all four settings).
note: The manipulated variables are the GW-defining computations themselves (broadcast property; unsupervised cycle-consistency objectives), each removed while the rest of the architecture is held fixed; the full GW's broadcast-plus-cycles computation carries the transfer function that its ablations lack.

justification_quote: Sec. 5 (Fig. 3; 'All results are averaged across five different runs... error bars reflect 95% confidence intervals computed via bootstrapping'; 2 environments x 2 data regimes): 'only policies trained from GW latents could systematically generalize to the opposite modality'; matched baselines (AVAE, CLIP-like, GW w/o cycles) fail zero-shot transfer in the majority or all settings.
note: Attribution to the GW mechanism rests on matched ablations (CLIP-like = contrastive alignment only; GW w/o cycles = supervised without cycles) and the AVAE baseline, with unimodal upper baselines per environment; CLIP-like is the designated non-broadcast control of the GW mechanism.

justification_quote: Gain shown across two environments (Factory, Simple Shapes), two data regimes (Full/Low), both transfer directions (attr->vis, vis->attr) in Fig. 3, and replicated with a second RL algorithm - App. E: 'the results are reproducible with this alternative algorithm' (Fig. 6, A2C).
note: Cross-environment, cross-regime, cross-direction and cross-algorithm evidence with own controls; both environments remain simple simulated settings, which the conclusion itself flags as a scope limit for real-world settings.

justification_quote: Abstract is explicitly scoped ('In two distinct environments and tasks, our results reveal the model's ability to perform zero-shot cross-modal transfer'); each abstract claim maps to a specific controlled comparison in Fig. 3, and the conclusion flags remaining scope limits (other modalities) rather than overclaiming.
note: scope_match = match: the zero-shot transfer claim and the ablation-failure claim ('Variants and ablations of the full Global Workspace... did not display the same generalization abilities') both match the demonstrated evidence scope.

justification_quote: Abstract's headline improvement is zero-shot cross-modal transfer that 'Variants and ablations of the full Global Workspace (including a CLIP-like multimodal representation trained via contrastive learning) did not display' - the claim rests on attributing the capability to the GW mechanism rather than to generic multimodal alignment.
